name: International Style
summary: Light rectilinear volumes of steel, glass and white render, with flat roofs, ribbon windows and free plans. The Bauhaus, Le Corbusier and Mies van der Rohe defined it in the 1920s, and it became the global language of the office tower.

philosophy.core_thesis: A building is a volume enclosed by a thin skin, and industrial methods make one rational form valid in every place.
design_principles: Treat the building as volume, not mass: wrap a structural frame in a thin, flat skin of glass or render.
Carry the loads on a regular grid of slender columns, so that walls are free partitions and the plan is open.
Order the facade by the regularity of the structural bay, not by axial symmetry.
Use horizontal ribbon windows or full-height glazing set flush with the wall plane.
Keep the roof flat and usable, and keep the eaves line free of cornices.
Remove applied ornament and rely on proportion and the precision of standard parts.
anti_patterns: Pitched roofs, gables, cornices or dormers
Applied ornament, classical orders or regional motifs
Thick load-bearing walls with small punched windows
Symmetric compositions around a ceremonial central axis
Rough, hand-made or strongly textured surfaces
Curved or free-form volumes that ignore the structural grid

massing.form: Simple orthogonal prisms, single or intersecting, with smooth planes and sharp arrises.
massing.proportion: Long horizontal bodies for houses and slabs; a regular bay of 4 to 7m repeated without a central emphasis.
massing.roof: Flat roof, often a terrace or roof garden, with a parapet that is level with the wall plane.
massing.relation_to_ground: The volume stands free on pilotis or on a recessed glass ground floor, so that the ground continues under it.

structure.system: A steel or reinforced-concrete skeleton with non-load-bearing curtain walls and partitions.
structure.span_and_module: A column grid of 4 to 9m, set back from the facade so that the skin runs past the columns without a break.
structure.expression: The grid is legible but restrained: slim mullions, expressed slab edges or steel I-sections mark the module.

materials.finish: Smooth, precise and machine-made; surfaces are painted, polished or glazed and show no trace of the hand.

facade.composition: A flat taut skin divided by a regular module; no part of the elevation projects more than the depth of a mullion.
facade.openings: Continuous ribbon windows, corner glazing or a full curtain wall, with frames as thin as the technology allows.
facade.solid_to_void: Void dominates on later work: 50–90% glass; early white villas hold about 30–40% glass in long bands.

light_and_space.daylight: Even, abundant daylight from floor-to-ceiling glazing; the interior reads as bright and shadowless.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: A free plan: space flows between screens and cores without closed corridors, and the inside continues to the outside through glass.
light_and_space.interior_character: White planes, exposed slender columns, built-in storage and tubular-steel furniture; few objects, placed with precision.

ornament.attitude: Ornament is rejected; the quality of proportion, joints and materials replaces it.

rules.rule: Repeat a regular structural grid over the whole front.
Leave the wall plain and white, with no applied ornament.
Set the volume on a clean ratio, and lift it on pilotis.
Balance the volumes without a mirror axis, and keep the front free.
Use the ribbon window to give a long horizontal view.

emotion.target_response: Clarity and progress: the viewer feels a rational, weightless order that belongs to no single place.

avoid_when: The brief asks for local character, craft or a strong response to climate.
The site needs heavy thermal mass or small openings.

modifiers.how: Thicken the frame, leave the concrete raw and set the windows deep; keep the flat roof and the regular bay.

sources.title: Henry-Russell Hitchcock and Philip Johnson, The International Style (W. W. Norton, 1932)
